analysis.one_liner: Lets employees at larger employers earn up to seven paid sick days a year.
analysis.headline: The bill won support from 155 House Democrats but was referred to three committees and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The Healthy Families Act would require employers with 15 or more workers to let employees earn one hour of paid sick time for every 30 hours worked, capped at 56 hours (seven days) a year. The time could cover a worker's own illness, a sick child or family member, or dealing with domestic violence. Employers with fewer than 15 workers could opt out of paying for it but would have to give 56 hours of unpaid sick time.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers without paid sick days, who are concentrated in low-wage jobs like food service, home care, and retail. The bill text cites figures showing 61 percent of the lowest-earning private-sector workers lack paid sick time, along with more than 80 percent of food preparation and serving workers. Workers who need time to recover from illness, care for a sick child, or handle domestic violence situations would gain guaranteed, protected leave.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-wage workers without paid sick days

how_it_helps.text: Employees earn one hour of paid sick time for every 30 hours worked, up to 56 hours a year, usable for their own illness, preventive care, caring for family members, or taking legal and safety steps related to domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking.
Employers cannot fire, retaliate against, or count sick days against workers under no-fault attendance policies, and workers can sue for lost wages and reinstatement, with attorney's fees available.

The bill's findings cite research linking paid sick days to fewer people working while sick, lower influenza rates in cities that adopted such laws, and roughly $1.1 billion a year in avoided emergency-room costs.
Employers that already offer equivalent paid leave are exempt from the new requirement, so the mandate falls mainly on businesses that currently provide no sick time.
The bill explicitly preserves more generous state and local sick leave laws, so workers in places like New York or San Francisco keep stronger protections.

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 15 or more employees, especially those in retail, restaurants, and other low-wage sectors that currently offer no paid sick leave, would pay the wages for sick days and manage recordkeeping and scheduling. Businesses that already provide comparable leave pay nothing new.
analysis.who_pays_short: Businesses without existing sick leave policies

drawbacks.text: The mandate is a new payroll cost for employers that currently provide no sick leave, and firms just above the 15-employee threshold face the same requirement as large corporations, a cliff that some employers say discourages hiring beyond the threshold.
Even many supporters of paid leave argue that sick time is better handled through broader family and medical leave programs, since seven capped days do not cover serious or long-term illness.
A federal floor could displace the flexibility some employers and workers negotiate, though the bill forbids the new right from weakening any existing contract or state law that is more generous.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is substantial and targeted: millions of workers who currently lose wages or their jobs when they get sick would gain paid time to recover or see a doctor, with documented public-health spillovers. The cost is a real but modest compliance burden on employers without existing leave policies, partially offset by reduced presenteeism, turnover, and emergency-room use. The main design weakness is the abrupt 15-employee threshold rather than a phase-in.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and the Workforce, House Administration, and Oversight and Government Reform committees on the day it was introduced, and none of them ever acted on it before the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Rosa DeLauro (D-CT) introduced the Healthy Families Act on March 13, 2017, and it was referred the same day to the Education and the Workforce Committee and, in addition, to the House Administration and Oversight and Government Reform committees.
155 House Democrats signed on as cosponsors; the cosponsor list shows no Republican support.
No hearing, markup, or vote was ever held in any of the three committees, and the bill never reached the House floor.
The Congress ended on January 3, 2019, so the bill died without action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that currently provide no paid sick leave were better off because the bill died, since they avoided the new wage and compliance obligation. Committee chairs kept discretion over whether any such mandate reaches a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers that provide no paid sick leave

for.name: Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 155 cosponsors for the earned paid sick time mandate.

for.name: 155 of 194 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including the House minority leader and committee ranking members.

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill — no hearing, markup, or vote — during the full two-year Congress.

against.name: House Administration and Oversight and Government Reform Committees
against.what_they_did: Also took no action on the bill during the Congress.

against.name: Retail, restaurant, and other business lobbies
against.role: Opponents of federal paid sick leave mandates
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal paid sick leave requirements on cost grounds, as they had in earlier Congresses; no opposition appears in the bill's committee record because the bill never received a hearing.

sides.party_line_note: All 155 cosponsors were House Democrats, and the committees controlled by the House Republican majority took no action on the bill.

industries.industry: Restaurants, retail, and other low-wage service employers
industries.note: These industries are the main employers of the roughly one-third of private-sector workers without paid sick time, so the mandate's cost would fall mostly on them. Their gain from the bill's death was avoiding a new wage obligation for leave they currently don't pay for.

industries.industry: Employers with existing paid leave policies
industries.note: They are exempt if their current policy meets the bill's standards, and the bill bars weakening any more generous contract or state law, so their costs are near zero and their workforce gains protection they already fund.

industries.industry: Healthcare providers and public health programs
industries.note: The bill's findings cite studies that paid sick days shift care from emergency rooms toward routine and preventive care, reducing costs for Medicare and Medicaid.
